title: The Representation Ring
---

What algebraic structure do the representations of a fixed finite group $G$ carry? On isomorphism classes of representations there are two operations, $\oplus$ and $\otimes$. Both are commutative and associative up to isomorphism, and $\otimes$ distributes over $\oplus$: $(X \oplus Y) \otimes Z \cong (X \otimes Z) \oplus (Y \otimes Z)$. (The isomorphisms of Propositions [9.8.8](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-8) and [9.9.3](/notes/math-55a/9-9-multilinear-maps-and-the-tensor-algebra#proposition-9-9-3) that express these laws are given by formulas such as $(x, y) \otimes z \mapsto (x \otimes z, y \otimes z)$, so they commute with the actions of $G$.) This is almost a ring; what is missing is additive inverses, and we add them formally.

:::definition{14.5.1} Representation ring
Let $\hat{R}$ be the free abelian group on the set of isomorphism classes $[X]$ of representations of $G$; its elements are finite formal sums $\sum_j c_j[X_j]$ with $c_j \in \ZZ$. The ***representation ring*** $R(G)$ is the quotient of $\hat{R}$ by the subgroup $N$ generated by all elements $[X] + [Y] - [X \oplus Y]$. Its multiplication is defined on generators by $[X] \cdot [Y] = [X \otimes Y]$ and extended bilinearly.
:::

The multiplication is well defined on $\hat R$, which is free on the classes $[X]$, and it descends to $R(G) = \hat{R}/N$ because $N$ is an ideal: $$\bigl([X] + [Y] - [X \oplus Y]\bigr)[Z] = [X \otimes Z] + [Y \otimes Z] - [(X \otimes Z) \oplus (Y \otimes Z)] \in N,$$ using $(X \oplus Y) \otimes Z \cong (X \otimes Z) \oplus (Y \otimes Z)$, and similarly for products on the other side. It is commutative, associative and distributive because $\otimes$ is, and its identity is the class $[U]$ of the trivial representation, since $U \otimes X \cong X$. In $R(G)$ we have $[X] + [Y] = [X \oplus Y]$, and now differences $[X] - [Y]$ also make sense.

:::proposition{14.5.2} The character map
The map $[X] \mapsto \chi_X$ induces an injective ring homomorphism $$\Psi : R(G) \to \CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G), \qquad \sum_i a_i[V_i] \mapsto \sum_i a_i\chi_i,$$ where $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ is a ring under pointwise addition and multiplication. The classes $[V_1], \ldots, [V_k]$ of the irreducible representations form a basis of the abelian group $R(G)$, so $(R(G), +) \cong \ZZ^k$, where $k$ is the number of conjugacy classes of $G$.
:::

:::proof
The homomorphism $\hat R \to \CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ sending each generator $[X]$ to $\chi_X$ vanishes on $N$ because $\chi_{X \oplus Y} = \chi_X + \chi_Y$, so it induces an additive map $\Psi$ on $R(G)$. It is multiplicative because $\chi_{X \otimes Y} = \chi_X\chi_Y$, and $\Psi([U]) = 1$. By complete reducibility, every representation satisfies $[X] = \sum_i a_i[V_i]$ in $R(G)$ with $a_i \geq 0$, so the classes $[V_i]$ generate $R(G)$ as an abelian group. If $\sum_i a_i[V_i] = 0$, then applying $\Psi$ gives $\sum_i a_i\chi_i = 0$, so all $a_i = 0$ because the $\chi_i$ are linearly independent. Hence the $[V_i]$ form a basis, and $\Psi$ is injective. Finally, $k$ is the number of conjugacy classes by Theorem [13.6.2](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#theorem-13-6-2).
:::

General elements $\sum_i a_i[V_i]$ of $R(G)$ are called ***virtual representations***. The actual representations, those with all $a_i \geq 0$, form a cone inside $R(G)\cong \ZZ^k$, that is, a subset closed under addition. The image of $\Psi$ is the lattice of ***virtual characters*** $\Lambda = \{\sum_i a_i\chi_i : a_i \in \ZZ\} \subset \CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$.

:::example{14.5.3} The representation ring of $S_3$
By Example [13.3.6](/notes/math-55a/13-3-schurs-lemma#example-13-3-6), $V \otimes V \cong U \oplus U' \oplus V$, and comparing characters gives $U' \otimes U' \cong U$ and $U' \otimes V \cong V$. So in $R(S_3)$, which has basis $[U], [U'], [V]$ and identity $[U]$, $$[U']^2 = [U], \qquad [U'][V] = [V], \qquad [V]^2 = [U] + [U'] + [V].$$
:::

What, then, is an arbitrary class function the character of? Allowing complex coefficients, let $R(G)_{\CC}$ be the complex vector space with basis $[V_1], \ldots, [V_k]$, with the multiplication of $R(G)$ extended bilinearly. The map $\Psi$ extends to a $\CC$-linear map $\Psi_{\CC} : R(G)_{\CC} \to \CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$, $\sum_i a_i[V_i] \mapsto \sum_i a_i\chi_i$ with $a_i \in \CC$, which is still multiplicative.

:::corollary{14.5.4} Class functions as virtual characters
The map $\Psi_{\CC} : R(G)_{\CC} \to \CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ is an isomorphism of $\CC$-algebras.
:::

:::proof
It is a multiplicative linear map that sends the basis $[V_1], \ldots, [V_k]$ of $R(G)_{\CC}$ to the basis $\chi_1, \ldots, \chi_k$ of $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ (Theorem [13.6.2](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#theorem-13-6-2)).
:::

:::note
The theorems of Artin and Brauer (Theorems [15.3.4](/notes/math-55a/15-3-frobenius-reciprocity#theorem-15-3-4) and [15.3.5](/notes/math-55a/15-3-frobenius-reciprocity#theorem-15-3-5)) describe the lattice $\Lambda$ of virtual characters inside $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ in terms of characters induced from subgroups of $G$.
:::

:::exercise{14.5.5} Character Tables and the Representation Ring
<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. Using the character table of $S_4$, show that $V \otimes V' \cong U' \oplus V \oplus V' \oplus W$.
2. Let $V$ be the standard representation of $S_5$. Show that $\bigwedge^3 V \cong V'$ by computing $\chi_{\bigwedge^3 V}$ from the formula $$\chi_{\bigwedge^3 V}(g) = \tfrac16\bigl(\chi_V(g)^3 - 3\chi_V(g)\chi_V(g^2) + 2\chi_V(g^3)\bigr),$$ and justify the formula.
3. Verify column orthogonality (Proposition [13.6.5](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#proposition-13-6-5)) for the character table of $A_5$.
4. Using the character table of $S_5$, decompose $\bigwedge^2 V \otimes U'$ and $V \otimes W$ into irreducibles.
5. Let $V_1, \ldots, V_k$ be the irreducible representations of $G$, and write $[V_i][V_j] = \sum_\ell n_{ij}^\ell[V_\ell]$ in $R(G)$. Show that the structure constants $n_{ij}^\ell$ are nonnegative integers, that $n_{ij}^\ell = n_{ji}^\ell$, and that $n_{ij}^\ell = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\chi_i(g)\,\chi_j(g)\,\ol{\chi_\ell(g)}$.
6. Let $V$ be the standard representation of $S_n$, $n \geq 2$. Show that $\bigwedge^{n-1} V \cong U'$.

:::solution
**(1)** The character of $V \otimes V'$ is $\chi_V\chi_{V'} = (9, -1, 1, 0, -1)$, in the order of the table. With the class sizes $1, 6, 3, 8, 6$, $$\begin{aligned}
H(\chi_U, \chi_V\chi_{V'}) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(9 - 6 + 3 + 0 - 6) = 0, \\
H(\chi_{U'}, \chi_V\chi_{V'}) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(9 + 6 + 3 + 0 + 6) = 1, \\
H(\chi_W, \chi_V\chi_{V'}) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(18 + 0 + 6 + 0 + 0) = 1, \\
H(\chi_V, \chi_V\chi_{V'}) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(27 - 6 - 3 + 0 + 6) = 1, \\
H(\chi_{V'}, \chi_V\chi_{V'}) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(27 + 6 - 3 + 0 - 6) = 1.
\end{aligned}$$ So $V \otimes V' \cong U' \oplus V \oplus V' \oplus W$, and the dimensions agree: $1 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 9$. Alternatively, $V \otimes V' = (V \otimes V) \otimes U' \cong (U \oplus V \oplus V' \oplus W) \otimes U'$, and $W \otimes U' \cong W$.

**(2)** If $g$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_4$ on $V$ with eigenvectors $v_1, \ldots, v_4$, the vectors $v_i \wedge v_j \wedge v_l$, $i < j < l$, form a basis of $\bigwedge^3 V$ of eigenvectors with eigenvalues $\lambda_i\lambda_j\lambda_l$ (Proposition [9.10.19](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-19)). Write $p_r = \sum_i\lambda_i^r = \chi_V(g^r)$ and $e_3 = \sum_{i<j<l}\lambda_i\lambda_j\lambda_l = \chi_{\bigwedge^3 V}(g)$. Expanding, $$\begin{aligned}
p_1^3 &= p_3 + 3\sum_{i \neq j}\lambda_i^2\lambda_j + 6e_3, \\
p_1p_2 &= p_3 + \sum_{i \neq j}\lambda_i^2\lambda_j,
\end{aligned}$$ so $p_1^3 - 3p_1p_2 = -2p_3 + 6e_3$, which is the formula. Next we need $\chi_V(g^3)$. Cubing the representatives: $(12)^3 = (12)$, $((12)(34))^3 = (12)(34)$, $(123)^3 = e$, $((123)(45))^3 = (45)$, $(1234)^3 = (1432)$ and $(12345)^3 = (14253)$. So, in the order of the table, $$\begin{aligned}
\chi_V(g) &= (4, 2, 0, 1, -1, 0, -1), \\
\chi_V(g^2) &= (4, 4, 4, 1, 1, 0, -1), \\
\chi_V(g^3) &= (4, 2, 0, 4, 2, 0, -1).
\end{aligned}$$ Entry by entry, $$\begin{aligned}
\chi_{\bigwedge^3 V} &= \tfrac16\bigl(64 - 48 + 8,\; 8 - 24 + 4,\; 0,\; 1 - 3 + 8,\; -1 + 3 + 4,\; 0,\; -1 - 3 - 2\bigr) \\
&= (4, -2, 0, 1, 1, 0, -1),
\end{aligned}$$ which is $\chi_{V'}$. So $\bigwedge^3 V \cong V'$.

**(3)** Write $\varphi = \frac{1 + \sqrt5}{2}$ and $\bar\varphi = \frac{1 - \sqrt5}{2}$, so that $\varphi + \bar\varphi = 1$ and $\varphi\bar\varphi = -1$; all entries are real. Using the rows $U, Y, Z, V, W$, the sums $\sum_i\chi_i(g_s)\chi_i(g_t)$ for $s = t$ are $$\begin{aligned}
e&: \ 1 + 9 + 9 + 16 + 25 = 60, & (12)(34)&: \ 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 4, \\
(123)&: \ 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 3, & \text{\(5\)-cycles}&: \ 1 + \varphi^2 + \bar\varphi^2 + 1 + 0 = 5,
\end{aligned}$$ using $\varphi^2 + \bar\varphi^2 = (\varphi + \bar\varphi)^2 - 2\varphi\bar\varphi = 3$ for either class of $5$-cycles. These are $60/1$, $60/15$, $60/20$ and $60/12$. For $s \neq t$: $$\begin{aligned}
e,\ (12)(34)&: \ 1 - 3 - 3 + 0 + 5 = 0, \\
e,\ (123)&: \ 1 + 0 + 0 + 4 - 5 = 0, \\
e,\ \text{\(5\)-cycles}&: \ 1 + 3(\varphi + \bar\varphi) - 4 + 0 = 0, \\
(12)(34),\ (123)&: \ 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 - 1 = 0, \\
(12)(34),\ \text{\(5\)-cycles}&: \ 1 - (\varphi + \bar\varphi) + 0 + 0 = 0, \\
(123),\ \text{\(5\)-cycles}&: \ 1 + 0 + 0 - 1 + 0 = 0,
\end{aligned}$$ and for the two classes of $5$-cycles, $1 + 2\varphi\bar\varphi + 1 + 0 = 0$.

**(4)** The character of $\bigwedge^2 V \otimes U'$ is $\chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}\sgn$. The odd classes are those of $(12)$, $(123)(45)$ and $(1234)$, and $\chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}$ vanishes on all three, so $\chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}\sgn = \chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}$ and $\bigwedge^2 V \otimes U' \cong \bigwedge^2 V$.

The character of $V \otimes W$ is $\chi_V\chi_W = (20, 2, 0, -1, -1, 0, 0)$. With the class sizes $1, 10, 15, 20, 20, 30, 24$, $$\begin{aligned}
H(\chi_U, \chi_V\chi_W) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(20 + 20 + 0 - 20 - 20) = 0, \\
H(\chi_{U'}, \chi_V\chi_W) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(20 - 20 + 0 - 20 + 20) = 0, \\
H(\chi_V, \chi_V\chi_W) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(80 + 40 + 0 - 20 + 20) = 1, \\
H(\chi_{V'}, \chi_V\chi_W) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(80 - 40 + 0 - 20 - 20) = 0, \\
H(\chi_W, \chi_V\chi_W) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(100 + 20 + 0 + 20 - 20) = 1, \\
H(\chi_{W'}, \chi_V\chi_W) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(100 - 20 + 0 + 20 + 20) = 1, \\
H(\chi_{\bigwedge^2 V}, \chi_V\chi_W) &= \tfrac{1}{120}(120 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0) = 1,
\end{aligned}$$ where we have omitted the last two classes, on which $\chi_V\chi_W$ vanishes. So $V \otimes W \cong V \oplus W \oplus W' \oplus \bigwedge^2 V$, of dimension $4 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 20$.

**(5)** We have $[V_i][V_j] = [V_i \otimes V_j]$, and by Corollary [13.5.6](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-6), $V_i \otimes V_j \cong \bigoplus_\ell V_\ell^{\oplus m_\ell}$ with $m_\ell = H(\chi_\ell, \chi_i\chi_j)$, a nonnegative integer. Since the $[V_\ell]$ form a basis of $R(G)$, $n_{ij}^\ell = m_\ell = H(\chi_\ell, \chi_i\chi_j) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g\ol{\chi_\ell(g)}\,\chi_i(g)\,\chi_j(g)$, which is symmetric in $i$ and $j$.

**(6)** Since $\dim V = n - 1$, the space $\bigwedge^{n-1} V$ is $1$-dimensional, and $\sigma \in S_n$ acts on it by $\det(\sigma|_V)$ (Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3)). The permutation representation is $\CC^n = U \oplus V$, so the permutation matrix of $\sigma$ is conjugate to a block-diagonal matrix with blocks $1$ and the matrix of $\sigma|_V$, and $\det(\sigma|_V)$ equals the determinant of the permutation matrix, which is $\sgn\sigma$ (Proposition [5.4.24](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#proposition-5-4-24)). So $\sigma$ acts on $\bigwedge^{n-1} V$ as multiplication by $\sgn\sigma$, and $\bigwedge^{n-1} V \cong U'$.
:::
:::
